llm_response.content:
Below is a concise, complete empirical plan tailored to the data and context you provided.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary strategy: Staggered difference-in-differences with event-study dynamics estimated using modern estimators that are valid under staggered, possibly heterogeneous effects (Sun–Abraham or Callaway–Sant’Anna).
- Why appropriate: States adopted wrongful discharge exceptions at different times; that exogenous policy timing provides quasi-experimental variation. We can leverage pre/post within-state changes relative to not-yet-treated (and never-treated) states and test for pretrends.
- Design extensions:
  - Event-study to assess dynamics and pretrends.
  - Industry-focused triple-difference (DDD) as a robustness design: compare changes in temporary help employment relative to closely related business services within a state over time, before/after adoption. DDD helps net out state-time shocks to the broader services sector.
  - Validate CPS micro evidence with QCEW state-quarter aggregates.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variables:
  - Three separate treatments, analyzed one at a time:
    1) Implied contract exception in effect in state s at time t
    2) Good faith exception in effect in state s at time t
    3) Public policy exception in effect in state s at time t
  - Code each as a 0/1 indicator by month (CPS) or quarter (QCEW), turning on at the first effective date of the doctrine in that state. If there are documented reversals, either (i) code the time-varying status month-by-month and use a windowed “stacked” event study around first adoption, or (ii) exclude reversal states in the main analysis and add them in robustness checks.
- Control group / counterfactual:
  - Not-yet-treated states at each event time (and never-treated states) using Sun–Abraham or Callaway–Sant’Anna comparison sets.
  - When estimating the effect of one doctrine, include controls for the concurrent presence of the other doctrines to reduce confounding.
- Treatment timing / event date:
  - Month of adoption from the legal database. For court decisions, use the month of decision (or first full month after); for statutes, use the effective date month.
- Outcomes:
  - CPS micro: indicator that individual is employed in temporary help services (SIC 7362 / NAICS 56132; use appropriate CPS industry code crosswalk).
  - QCEW: state-level temporary help employment share of total employment; and within-business-services share as a robustness outcome.
- DDD robustness:
  - Construct a state-month panel of shares: temporary help share within business services (temp help / [temp help + other administrative and business services excluding temp help]) and compare treated vs control states; or at the micro level, restrict to workers in business services (temp help vs closely related services) and estimate a DDD.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends: In the absence of adoption, treated and control states would have followed similar trends in temporary help employment. Plausible? Moderately plausible: adoption was driven by court decisions and varied legal doctrines, not primarily by staffing market trends. We will test this with event-study leads and include rich controls.
- No anticipatory behavior affecting outcomes before the effective date: Firms are unlikely to shift to temp help materially before the doctrine is settled, though some anticipation is possible around oral arguments or legislative debate. We will examine pretrends and use narrow event windows as a check.
- Stable treatment and SUTVA: No cross-state spillovers (e.g., firms moving hiring across borders selectively). Likely small at the monthly horizon, but we will check sensitivity excluding small states and those with high cross-border commuting.
- No concurrent confounders perfectly collinear with adoption: Control for contemporaneous macro and compositional shifts (unemployment, manufacturing share, unionization, demographics) and include state and time fixed effects; also consider state-specific linear trends.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Endogenous adoption correlated with labor market shifts:
  - Mitigation: Event-study pretrend tests; state-specific linear trends; include rich time-varying controls; region-by-time fixed effects; robustness restricting to court-adopted changes only (excluding statutory adoptions) to reduce policy endogeneity.
- Industry measurement issues in CPS (industry code changes over time; misclassification of temp help early in the sample):
  - Mitigation: Use consistent crosswalks across coding changes; restrict to wage-and-salary workers; verify results with QCEW (which directly measures industry employment) and with outcome defined as temp help share within business services to reduce compositional effects.
- Concurrency of multiple doctrines:
  - Mitigation: Estimate each doctrine separately, controlling for the presence of the others; also estimate an index (0–3 exceptions in force) as a robustness; use event-study to see which doctrine “moves” outcomes.
- Reversals or partial implementation:
  - Mitigation: Exclude reversal states in baseline; include them in robustness using windowed/stacked designs centered on first adoption.

5. R Code Outline
Note: This is an executable outline; adapt variable names to your files. It shows (i) CPS micro event study for implied contract, (ii) QCEW validation, and (iii) a DDD-style robustness using shares within business services.

# Packages
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)        # Sun-Abraham via sunab()
library(did)           # Callaway-Sant'Anna robustness
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Load data
cps <- fread("cps_monthly_1979_1995.csv")       # Individual-level CPS
laws <- fread("state_wd_law_dates.csv")         # Adoption dates by state and doctrine
controls <- fread("state_controls_monthly.csv") # Unemp, manuf share, union, demo by state-month
qcew <- fread("qcew_state_quarterly.csv")       # State x quarter, temp help employment, total emp

# 2) Prepare CPS micro data
# Assumed columns: state (2-letter or FIPS), year, month, age, empstat, classwkr, weight,
#                  industry codes (sic or naics or census_ind), sex, educ, race
cps[, ym := ym(year, month)]
cps <- cps[age >= 16 & age <= 64]                       # prime-ish ages
cps <- cps[empstat == "employed" & classwkr == "private_wage_salary"]  # exclude self-employed/gov

# Identify temp help industry (adjust to your coding scheme)
# Example handles multiple possibilities; adapt to your variable names
temphelp_codes_census <- c(739)  # placeholder; replace with actual Census industry code(s) for temp help
cps[, temp_help := 0L]
if ("sic" %in% names(cps)) cps[sic == 7362, temp_help := 1L]
if ("naics" %in% names(cps)) cps[naics == 56132, temp_help := 1L]
if ("census_ind" %in% names(cps)) cps[census_ind %in% temphelp_codes_census, temp_help := 1L]

# 3) Merge in wrongful discharge adoption dates
# laws expected columns: state, implied_date, goodfaith_date, publicpolicy_date (Date or year-month)
for (v in c("implied_date","goodfaith_date","publicpolicy_date")) {
  if (!inherits(laws[[v]], "Date")) laws[, (v) := as.Date(paste0(v), origin="1970-01-01")]
}
# Create monthly event dates
laws[, implied_ym := ym(year(implied_date), month(implied_date))]
laws[, goodfaith_ym := ym(year(goodfaith_date), month(goodfaith_date))]
laws[, public_ym := ym(year(publicpolicy_date), month(publicpolicy_date))]

cps <- merge(cps, laws[, .(state, implied_ym, goodfaith_ym, public_ym)], by="state", all.x=TRUE)

# Treatment indicators by doctrine (time-varying)
cps[, treat_implied := as.integer(!is.na(implied_ym) & ym >= implied_ym)]
cps[, treat_goodfaith := as.integer(!is.na(goodfaith_ym) & ym >= goodfaith_ym)]
cps[, treat_public := as.integer(!is.na(public_ym) & ym >= public_ym)]

# Cohort variables (first treat date for Sun-Abraham)
# Non-adopters get NA/Inf; fixest sunab handles not-yet-treated appropriately
cps[, g_implied := implied_ym]  # cohort = first month of implied adoption

# 4) Merge state-month controls
controls[, ym := ym(year, month)]
cps <- merge(cps, controls[, .(state, ym, unemp_rate, manuf_share, union_rate,
                               share_age_16_24, share_college, share_female, share_black)],
             by=c("state","ym"), all.x=TRUE)

# 5) Main event-study: CPS micro, implied contract as treatment
# Outcome: indicator employed in temp help
# FE: state and month-year; Controls: state-level covariates; Cluster: state; Weights: CPS weights
# Sun-Abraham: sunab(cohort, time) with not-yet-treated as control set
est_cps_implied <- feols(
  temp_help ~ sunab(g_implied, ym) +
    unemp_rate + manuf_share + union_rate +
    share_age_16_24 + share_college + share_female + share_black +
    treat_goodfaith + treat_public,   # control for concurrent doctrines
  data = cps,
  weights = ~ weight,                 # CPS person weight
  cluster = ~ state,
  fixef = ~ state + ym
)

# Plot dynamic effects
iplot(est_cps_implied, ref.line = 0, main = "Event study: Implied contract -> Temp help employment")

# 6) Simple post-period ATT (optional)
# Collapse Sun-Abraham post coefficients into average post effect
agg_cps_implied <- aggte(est_cps_implied, type = "dynamic")  # fixest provides iplot; for ATT, use did on aggregates below

# 7) Callaway–Sant’Anna robustness on CPS (state x month)
# Build state-month panel outcome: temp help employment share in CPS (weighted)
cps_sm <- cps[, .(temp_help_share = weighted.mean(temp_help, weight),
                  N = .N),
              by = .(state, ym, g_implied, treat_implied)]
cps_sm <- merge(cps_sm, controls[, .(state, ym, unemp_rate, manuf_share, union_rate,
                                     share_age_16_24, share_college, share_female, share_black)],
                by=c("state","ym"), all.x=TRUE)

# did::att_gt expects group (cohort) and time as integers; create year-month index
cps_sm[, time_id := as.integer(ym)]
# Group: first treat time id; for never-treated, keep NA and did will handle via control_group="notyettreated"
cps_sm[, group := ifelse(is.na(g_implied), -1L, as.integer(g_implied))]

att_cps_implied <- att_gt(yname = "temp_help_share",
                          tname = "time_id",
                          idname = "state",
                          gname = "group",
                          xformla = ~ unemp_rate + manuf_share + union_rate +
                                     share_age_16_24 + share_college + share_female + share_black,
                          data = cps_sm,
                          control_group = "notyettreated",
                          clustervars = "state")
es_cps_implied <- aggte(att_cps_implied, type = "dynamic")
summary(es_cps_implied)
# plot(es_cps_implied)  # dynamic ATT by relative time

# 8) QCEW validation (state-quarter)
qcew[, yq := paste0(year,"Q", quarter)]
# Outcomes: log temp help employment share
qcew[, temp_share := temp_help_emp / total_emp]
qcew <- merge(qcew, laws[, .(state, implied_ym)], by="state", all.x=TRUE)
# Map quarter to month for cohort alignment (use first month of quarter)
qcew[, ym := ym(year, (quarter - 1) * 3 + 1)]
qcew[, g_implied := implied_ym]
qcew[, treat_implied := as.integer(!is.na(implied_ym) & ym >= implied_ym)]

est_qcew_implied <- feols(
  log(temp_share + 1e-6) ~ sunab(g_implied, ym) +
    unemp_rate + manuf_share + union_rate,
  data = qcew,
  cluster = ~ state,
  fixef = ~ state + ym
)
iplot(est_qcew_implied, ref.line=0, main="Event study (QCEW): Implied -> log temp help share")

# 9) DDD-style robustness: temp help share within business services (state-month)
# Build business services bucket (adjust to coding). Assume we have census_ind; define biz services excl. temp help.
biz_other_codes <- c(738, 736)  # placeholder: adjust to business/administrative support excluding temp help
cps[, biz_other := as.integer(census_ind %in% biz_other_codes & temp_help == 0)]
cps_biz <- cps[temp_help == 1 | biz_other == 1]

cps_biz_sm <- cps_biz[, .(
  emp_temp = sum(weight * (temp_help == 1)),
  emp_biz_other = sum(weight * (biz_other == 1))
), by = .(state, ym)]
cps_biz_sm[, share_temp_within_biz := emp_temp / pmax(emp_temp + emp_biz_other, 1e-6)]

cps_biz_sm <- merge(cps_biz_sm, laws[, .(state, implied_ym)], by="state", all.x=TRUE)
cps_biz_sm[, g_implied := implied_ym]
cps_biz_sm[, treat_implied := as.integer(!is.na(implied_ym) & ym >= implied_ym)]
cps_biz_sm <- merge(cps_biz_sm, controls[, .(state, ym, unemp_rate, manuf_share, union_rate)],
                    by=c("state","ym"), all.x=TRUE)

ddd_est <- feols(
  share_temp_within_biz ~ sunab(g_implied, ym) + unemp_rate + manuf_share + union_rate,
  data = cps_biz_sm,
  fixef = ~ state + ym,
  cluster = ~ state
)
iplot(ddd_est, ref.line=0, main="DDD proxy: share temp within business services")

# 10) Additional robustness suggestions (implement as needed):
# - Add state-specific linear trends to main models: fixef = ~ state + ym | add state-specific trend via feols argument "ssc" or include interactions of state with a linear time index.
# - Exclude states with reversals.
# - Placebo: Use “fake” adoption dates shifted earlier to test for spurious pre-effects.

6. Expected Results
- Direction: Positive. Stronger wrongful discharge protections increase the costs/risks of directly employing and dismissing workers, incentivizing outsourcing to temporary help agencies.
- Magnitude (prior): For implied contract, an increase in temporary help employment share on the order of 0.1–0.3 percentage points within 3–5 years post-adoption (relative to a late 1970s base of <0.5%), i.e., roughly 20–60% relative growth from baseline. Good faith (rarer but stronger) could have somewhat larger effects; public policy is narrower, so smaller effects are expected.
- Dynamics: Likely gradual ramp-up over 1–4 years as firms adjust hiring practices and as staffing firms expand supply.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/event study)
- C1: Credible counterfactual trends validated by pretrends (event-study leads) — 1 if pretrends flat; otherwise 0. Currently: 1 contingent on tests.
- C2: Correct handling of staggered adoption (avoid TWFE bias) — 1 (Sun–Abraham / C&S estimators).
- C3: No anticipation / limited pre-treatment effects — 1 if leads near zero; currently 1 with verification.
- C4: No major time-varying confounders aligned with adoption — 1 with rich controls, state FE, time FE, region-time FE and trends; residual risk remains but mitigated.
- C5: SUTVA/no spillovers across states — 0.5 to 1; likely small, but cannot fully rule out. I assign 0.5.

Notes on implementation details
- Analyze doctrines separately with controls for other doctrines’ status. Report dynamic effects, average 0–2y, 3–5y windows.
- Weight CPS regressions by person weights; cluster SEs at state.
- Harmonize CPS industry codes across recodes; validate with QCEW.
- Sensitivity:
  - Add state-specific linear trends.
  - Exclude early/late adopters.
  - Court-driven adoptions only.
  - Alternative outcomes: part-time share, temp help among newly hired (if observed) to explore mechanisms.
